title: Do You Want Us to Pull Them Up?
subtitle: The servants' itch, the Master's No, and why a life is never called early
teaser: The servants got the diagnosis exactly right and the verdict exactly early. Nobody can tell wheat from weeds mid-season — least of all in the life you love and grieve — and the Master's No uses the same verb as 'forgive.'
theme: Building day: why no life is called early — and who the Master's patience is holding the field open for
framework: Matthew 13:30 - Let both grow together until the harvest

modules.passage: 'An enemy did this,' he replied. So the servants asked him, 'Do you want us to go and pull them up?' 'No,' he said, 'if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.'
emphasis: Do you want us to go and pull them up?
Let both grow together until the harvest
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes with the exchange at the parable's center — the offer, and the No.

modules.definition: let, permit, leave — the imperative of aphiēmi, Matthew's verb for FORGIVE
modules.usage: "Let both grow together" — the command is built on the same Greek verb the Lord's Prayer uses for forgive: aphes hēmin, forgive us our debts. The patience of the field is forgiveness-shaped — never indifference wearing overalls — and it is still covering the person you love who has not yet turned.

modules.prompt: Is there someone you love whose file you have quietly closed — the one who, today, wants nothing to do with God — and how sure are you, really, that their season is over?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Master of the field, my hands are quicker than Yours and my eyes are worse. Before I pull anyone up today — before I call any life finished, especially the one I love — teach me the verb You chose: let. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That was a whole reading. Below: why the servants were right about everything except the sickle, the church fathers who heard mercy inside the Master's No — and the slave trader whose life looked like weed for decades, until it turned out God was not finished with him.

modules.passage: The owner's servants came to him and said, 'Sir, didn't you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?' 'An enemy did this,' he replied. So the servants asked him, 'Do you want us to go and pull them up?' 'No,' he said, 'if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest. At that time I will tell the harvesters: First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.'
modules.greekOriginal: ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι ἀμφότερα ἕως τοῦ θερισμοῦ
modules.transliteration: aphete synauxanesthai amphotera heōs tou therismou — "let both grow together until the harvest"
emphasis: Let both grow together until the harvest
modules.scriptureContext: The dialogue at the parable's hinge: right diagnosis, wrong prescription, and a No that will take the rest of the week to understand.

modules.definition: to grow together — to increase side by side
modules.usage: This word appears exactly once in the New Testament: here. The kingdom's crop, in Jesus' telling, does not mature in a greenhouse. It grows up entangled — root to root with what opposes it — and reaches harvest anyway. Purity of environment is not a condition of the wheat's survival.
modules.usageNote: Pair it with the command that governs it: ἄφετε (aphete), the imperative of ἀφίημι (aphiēmi, G863) — release, permit, leave, and, throughout Matthew, FORGIVE: ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν, 'forgive us our debts' (6:12). Jesus could have chosen a colorless word for 'allow.' He chose the forgiveness verb. The field's long patience and the disciple's daily pardon are cut from the same cloth.

relatedWords.meaning: "forgive us" — the same verb, four chapters earlier, on every disciple's lips

modules.heading: The Most Reasonable Offer in the Gospels
modules.content:
Give the servants their due: everything about their offer is admirable. They noticed the weeds early. They went to the owner instead of acting alone. They asked before pulling. And their proposal is the most reasonable sentence in the parable: do you want us to go and pull them up? It is loyal, energetic, protective of the wheat, and aimed at the enemy's work. If you had been standing in that field, you would have raised your hand too.

Which is exactly why the Master's answer lands like cold water: No.

Be honest about how strange that is. Yesterday's verses established that the weeds are real, hostile, and deliberately planted. Nobody in this story is confused about whether darnel is bad. And still the owner refuses the one action that every instinct — agricultural, moral, religious — demands. He does not deny the problem. He denies the servants the solution.

You know this itch from the inside, because it is the most spiritual-feeling impulse you own. The person poisoning your church: surely naming and expelling them is service. The corrupt leader, the toxic relative, the online enemy of everything good: surely zeal against them is zeal for God. The servants' offer is the ancestor of every purge, every crusade, every write-off ever launched in the Owner's name — and before we can hear why He says No, we have to feel how sincerely we would have made the offer. Notice, too, what the offer always is underneath: a verdict on people, passed mid-season, by workers who cannot yet tell the crops apart. Today is the day the week gets personal — and not, first, about your enemies. The sharpest sickle most of us carry is a quiet one: the verdict already passed on someone we love. A brother who has told you plainly he does not believe. A father who changes the subject whenever it comes up. A friend who used to pray and now rolls her eyes at all of it. Somewhere along the way you stopped asking whether their season was over and started assuming it was — and that assumption is the servants' offer, made softly, without ever leaving your chair.
He does not deny the problem. He denies the servants the solution.

modules.heading: Three Reasons for the No
modules.content:
The Master gives one reason aloud, and the parable's details supply two more. Take them in order.

The stated reason: entangled roots. If you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. In a real field this is simple mechanics — darnel and wheat, sown together, root together; yank one and soil, roots, and neighboring stalks come up in the same fist. In the field of persons the mechanics are truer still. Lives are root-tangled: households, churches, friendships, histories. There is no surgical strike against a human being. You cannot rip a person out — of the field, or even of your hope — without tearing what God is still doing around them and through them. Every purge in history has advertised precision and harvested wheat by the armful — ask anyone who grew up in a church split that was going to finally purify the fellowship, or a movement that ate its own founders in the name of cleanness.

The first unstated reason: the servants cannot tell. Yesterday's botany returns with force. Darnel is wheat's near-twin until the heads form — and heads form only at the season's end. The servants proposing the weeding are the workers least equipped to perform it, not because they are wicked but because the information does not exist yet. Carry that into the field of persons and it lands harder still: you do not yet know who is actually faithful in God's kingdom. The rough-edged stranger may be wheat coming up the hard way; the polished stalk in the next pew may not be what it appears. And a life can look like weed for sixty years and still be gathered in as wheat at the end — nothing about a stalk's worst season settles its harvest. All week the parable has been drawing this line quietly: identification is a harvest-time skill, and it belongs to harvest-time workers.

The second unstated reason: the timing is load-bearing. Until the harvest is doing more than scheduling a delay: it IS the plan. Even Psalm 1 — Scripture's starkest sorting poem, the righteous tree against the wind-blown chaff — ends not with the righteous doing the sorting but with this: the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous. The Old Testament's own two-ways theology reserves the final telling-apart for God. The Master's No is that reservation, spoken into a field.

And underneath all three reasons, the verb glows. Let both grow — aphete. Matthew's forgiveness word, conjugated as farm policy. The No to the servants does not mean the Owner has gone soft on darnel. He is running His field the way He runs His pardon: absorbing the cost of evil's presence, for a season, on purpose, with his eyes open, for the sake of who can still be saved — including, perhaps, the very person whose name tightened your chest a few minutes ago.

modules.heading: Ancient Truth, Modern Life
modules.ancientTruth: The servants saw real weeds, named a real enemy — and were still refused the sickle, because identification and separation belong to the harvest and its appointed workers.
modules.modernApplication: Our tools have improved on the servants' offer: the exposure thread, the purity purge, the block-and-write-off, the church hunt for a congregation with no darnel in it — and, quieter than all of these, the settled sigh over someone we love: they will never change. The itch is identical; only the sickles are new.
modules.connectionPoint: Notice what the Master never says: he never says the servants' anger at the weeds is wrong. He redirects its verb. The energy that wants to uproot is invited to keep farming — water the wheat, watch the field, trust the No. Zeal is not the sin; jurisdiction is.
modules.newTestamentEcho: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." — Matthew 6:12 (BSB): the same verb (aphiēmi) that lets both grow. The verb you pray over your own debts is the verb He commands over your verdicts on other people.

modules.heading: The Reason Under the Reasons
modules.content:
The early church, reading this parable in centuries when it had every reason to want a sickle, heard something deeper under the Master's No — a hint the text leaves half-buried until you remember who is telling it.

John Chrysostom, preaching through Matthew in the fourth century, put it plainly: "Either He means this, If you are to take up arms, and to kill the heretics, many of the saints also must needs be overthrown with them; or that of the very tares it is likely that many may change and become wheat. If therefore ye root them up beforehand, you injure that which is to become wheat, slaying some, in whom there is yet room for change and improvement." Read that second clause again. In a real field, darnel is darnel until it dies. In THIS field, the tares can change kind. Chrysostom pressed the point to its edge — and kept both edges: "So long as they stand by the wheat, we must spare them, for it is possible for them even to become wheat; but when they have departed, having profited nothing, then of necessity the inexorable punishment will overtake them." The door stands open, and the door closes: mercy with a deadline is still mercy — and still a deadline.

Augustine, a generation later, said it with a preacher's economy: "I say this to the evil, who yet are Christians; I say this to the tares. For they are in the field; and it may so be, that they who to-day are tares, may to-morrow be wheat." And when a rigorist movement in North Africa demanded a purified church NOW — a field with the mixture already removed — Augustine answered from this same image: the Lord's threshing-floor "must needs contain, up to the time of the final winnowing, both grain which is to be stored in the garner, and chaff that is to be burned up with fire."

Here, then, is the reason under the reasons. The Master's No is ambition, not resignation. Every season the field stays mixed is a season the darnel is being given to defect. The patience that scandalizes the servants is aimed precisely at the stalks they wanted to burn — which means the uprooting they offered would not merely have cost some wheat. It would have foreclosed every future conversion in the field. Hold that beside the person you love who denies Him today: every season the sickle waits is a season the door stands open for exactly such a life. Say it in church-history terms: a sickle taken to the field in the late 1740s harvests a young slave-trading sailor named John Newton as darnel, and no one ever sings Amazing Grace.

Be honest about the record, too: the church has not always listened to its own fathers here. The same centuries that copied out Chrysostom's homily also built inquisitions; the parable's No has been read aloud by people sharpening sickles. That record argues not for softening the text but for keeping it sharp: every generation's servants make the same reasonable offer, and the Master's answer has not changed.

modules.inlineImageCaption: Below the surface the roots are already tangled — uprooting the one would tear out the other.

modules.heading: The Darnel That Wrote the Hymn
modules.content:
By any field inspection conducted in the 1740s, John Newton was darnel — and not ambiguously. A press-ganged sailor turned slave-trader, he had even been, in his own words, "in effect, though without the name, a Captive and a Slave myself" on the African coast. If ever a stalk deserved pulling, it was this one.

Then came the storm. "The 10th (that is, in the present style, the 21st) of March, is a day much to be remembered by me," he wrote, "and I have never suffered it to pass wholly unnoticed since the year 1748. On that day the Lord sent from on high, and delivered me out of deep waters." He had pumped the flooding ship from three in the morning until noon and steered her until midnight, praying for the first time in years. But here the story refuses to become the clean conversion tale we want — and its honesty is the point. The newly praying Newton went back to the trade. He sailed from Liverpool in 1750 as commander of a slave ship and made three voyages as captain, holding worship on deck "twice every Lord's day, officiating myself," while the hold beneath him carried its cargo. "I never had a scruple upon this head at the time," he confessed later, "nor was such a thought once suggested to me, by any friend." Only a sudden fit in 1754, the day before a fourth voyage, took him off the ships — not conviction; illness.

The wheat in him grew slowly — by decades, not seasons — tangled root to root with the darnel of his age and his own seared conscience. In time came ordination, the little parish of Olney, and the hymn the whole world knows. And forty years after the storm, the old pastor finally published his confession against the trade: "a public confession, which, however sincere, comes too late to prevent, or repair, the misery and mischief to which I have, formerly, been accessary… I was, once, an active instrument, in a business at which my heart now shudders." He lived just long enough to see Britain abolish that trade in 1807.

Run the field inspection at any single point in Newton's life — the trader on the coast, the praying captain above the hold, the man a sudden fit rather than conviction finally took off the ships — and the verdict comes back weed, decade after decade of it. Anyone who loved him would have had a lifetime of evidence for closing the file, and would have been wrong, because the God of this field was not finished. Only the whole season — the one no servant could see and no sickle would have spared — turns out to have been growing wheat the entire time.
modules.connectionToTheme: Newton is Chrysostom's clause with a biography: of the very tares it is likely that many may change and become wheat. Every premature uprooting forecloses an Amazing Grace. The Master's No was aimed at exactly this stalk — and it is still aimed at the stalks you have loved longest and hoped over least.

modules.heading: A Word Used Once
modules.content: Synauxanesthai — grow together — occurs exactly once in the New Testament, in the Master's No. Scripture needed the word only here, for only this policy: the kingdom's crop maturing side by side, root to root, with what opposes it. There is no greenhouse in the Gospels. The people growing around you are growing in contested soil, entangled and unfinished — and no mid-season glance can read a stalk's harvest identity: not a stranger's, and not that of the one you love.
modules.historicalContext: The command governing it, aphete, appears across Matthew as 'leave,' 'let,' and 'forgive' — one verb doing the work of release in fields, debts, and hearts alike.

modules.heading: Retiring Your Sickle
modules.content:
The servants' offer comes in three modern models. Check your shed for each.

The write-off. Somewhere in your life is a person you have harvested early — filed as darnel, verdict closed. For many of us the name in that file belongs to no enemy at all but to someone we love: the one who waves the whole subject away, who walked out of faith years ago and never looked back. Grief closed that file, not malice — which is why it is so hard to notice that it is closed. The parable does not ask you to trust them, excuse them, or restore what wisdom fences off. It asks you to reopen one file: the future. Chrysostom's clause — room for change and improvement — is the actual policy of the field's Owner, not a sentimentality, and Newton is that policy exercised across decades of weed-looking years. Practically: take the person you love whose life you have most quietly called early and pray for them once today as possible wheat. You are not declaring them safe. You are declaring the season unfinished — because a life is never called early, and theirs has not been called at all.

The purity search. Some believers spend years church-shopping for a field with no darnel — leaving each congregation at the first sighting of hypocrisy, certain the clean field exists one move away. The parable closes that road gently: both grow together until the harvest is the condition of every field this side of the barn. A church with visible weeds matches the only kind of field the parable describes. (Discernment survives this — Jesus will teach confronting a brother privately in chapter 18, and shepherds still guard flocks. Between correction and uprooting there is a canyon, and the No applies to the canyon's far side.)

The confident roster. Subtlest of all: the two-column ledger most of us keep without ever writing it down — this one is solid, that one is suspect; this friend is wheat, that coworker is weeds. The parable bankrupts the ledger from both sides. Since darnel and wheat cannot be told apart until the heads form, the stranger you filed under weeds may be wheat coming up slowly — and the polished stalk you certified years ago may be nothing of the kind. You do not know who is actually faithful in God's kingdom yet; neither did the servants, which is why the sorting was never assigned to them. Practically: catch yourself mid-sort once today, and over the person's name write the only verdict the field allows this early in the season: still growing.

One discipline serves all three: when the itch comes — and it will come today — convert it. The energy that wants to pull is real energy; the Master simply redirects its verb. Water something. Encourage something. Confront, if you must, the way chapter 18 teaches. But leave the sickle on the wall. The field's plan has a date for it, and harvest hands assigned.

modules.passage: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the Lord; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away. Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. For the Lord knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish.
emphasis: For the Lord knoweth the way of the righteous
modules.scriptureContext: The Old Testament's two-ways poem — tree and chaff — which still hands the final telling-apart to the LORD, not the righteous.

modules.prompt: Which of the three sickles is hanging in your shed — the write-off, the purity search, or the confident roster — and what would 'let both grow' cost you this week?
additionalQuestions: The servants' offer felt like loyalty. Where does your itch to uproot feel most like service to God?
Name — just to yourself — the person you love who is farthest from God. What changes this week if their life is mid-season rather than settled?
Someone once gave you the season you needed. Who was it, and have you ever thanked God for their withheld sickle?

modules.heading: Today's Practice: The Unfinished File
modules.instruction: A journaling exercise. Ten minutes, pen and paper — handwriting slows the verdicts down.

steps.title: Name the harvest you ran
steps.description: Write the name of the person you have most completely written off — for many of us, someone loved and far from God — and beneath it, the verdict you passed and roughly when you passed it.

steps.title: Reopen one file
steps.description: Under the verdict, copy Chrysostom's clause: 'it is possible for them even to become wheat.' Do not argue with it. Just let it sit under the name.

steps.title: Write the season you were given
steps.description: Now write two or three sentences about your own weediest stretch — and who, human or divine, declined to uproot you during it.

steps.title: Close with the verb
steps.description: End the page with one word, written large: aphete. Date it.

modules.heading: The Itch, Answered
modules.content:
We began with the most reasonable offer in the Gospels — loyal, protective, aimed at real evil — and the No that meets it.

By now the No has shown its inner workings: roots too tangled for surgical pulling, eyes too early for telling twins apart, a schedule where the delay is doing saving work, and under it all a verb borrowed from the vocabulary of pardon. None of it makes the Master soft on darnel. All of it makes Him serious about wheat — including the wheat still wearing darnel's face, the Newtons mid-season, the tares with defection in their future. Which means you do not know anyone's harvest identity yet: not the stranger's, not the pew-neighbor's, and not — hear this gently — that of the person you love who, today, still says no. Their harvest has not been called, because no harvest is called early, and none is called by servants.

Tomorrow Jesus takes the disciples indoors and decodes the whole story Himself — field, enemy, harvest, and the startling identity of the reapers. Tonight, one question is enough: the offer the servants made, you have made. The No they received, you have now received. What will you do with the energy in your sickle hand? The field's answer is already growing all around you: water something instead. And for the one you love, take this home tonight — the No that frustrated the servants is the same No still holding the field open over their life. Every day the sickle stays on the wall, the door stays open. The harvest was never in danger. It was never yours to secure.

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Master of the field, I confess the itch: I have offered You my sickle more often than my watering can. Thank You for the No that spared the people I would have pulled — and for the No that spared me, in the seasons when better eyes than mine could not have told what I was becoming. And for the one I love who denies You — keep Your field open over them, and keep my hope open with it; let me water while You wait. Teach me Your verb: aphete. Let me leave what You are letting grow, and love what You are still saving. Through Jesus, who spoke the No and paid for it. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Inhale: Let both grow — Exhale: until the harvest.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will name the person I love whose life I had quietly called early, reopen their file with one prayer for them as possible wheat, and convert today's uprooting energy into one concrete act of watering.

modules.heading: Community Reflection
modules.question: "Let both grow together" — the command ἄφετε (aphete) is built on the same Greek verb that Matthew's Gospel uses for what?
options: To forgive — as in 'forgive us our debts' (Matthew 6:12)
To judge at the proper time
modules.explanation: Aphete is the imperative of aphiēmi (G863) — release, leave, permit, and throughout Matthew, forgive. The Master's field policy and the disciple's daily pardon share one verb: the patience of the mixed field is forgiveness-shaped.

modules.heading: A Voice From the Story
modules.name: John Chrysostom
modules.bio: The 'golden-mouthed' preacher of the early church, whose verse-by-verse homilies through Matthew remain among the oldest complete expositions we possess. Made archbishop of Constantinople against his will, he preached against the excesses of court and clergy until the empire exiled him — twice. He died on the second forced march. A man who knew what it was to be treated as darnel by the field's self-appointed inspectors preached, in Homily 46, the parable's mercy with both edges intact.
modules.keyQuote: So long as they stand by the wheat, we must spare them, for it is possible for them even to become wheat.
modules.lessonForUs: Chrysostom heard in the Master's No both a shield for the saints and an open door for the tares — and the church that exiled him proved how badly every generation needs the reminder.

resources.description: Source of both Chrysostom quotations, verbatim from the NPNF text: the danger of overthrowing saints with heretics, and the tares' possibility of becoming wheat. Free at ccel.org and newadvent.org.

resources.title: Augustine, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament, Sermon XXIII §§3-4 — NPNF First Series Vol. 6 (trans. MacMullen); and Letter 185 (On the Correction of the Donatists) §15
resources.description: Source of 'they who to-day are tares, may to-morrow be wheat' and the threshing-floor answer to the Donatist demand for a purified church before the final winnowing.

resources.title: John Newton — primary sources
resources.description: An Authentic Narrative (1764), Letters VIII, XIII-XIV — the storm of March 21, 1748 kept as a lifelong anniversary, the three post-conversion voyages as slave-ship captain with Sunday worship on deck, and the 1754 illness that ended them; Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade (1788) — his published confession, quoted verbatim. His later pastorate and hymnody are documented record. The six post-conversion trading years are kept in this telling because Newton's own texts insist on them.

resources.title: Greek data
resources.description: aphete / aphiēmi (G863, the Matthew 6:12 forgiveness verb), synauxanesthai (G4885, NT hapax) — BibleHub interlinear and Strong's, Matthew 13:30.
